fields.expected: Most of my AI work has been on retrieval, agents, and evaluation. In Gloria I built the retrieval layer with OpenAI embeddings, Pinecone vector search, and a Neo4j graph to represent memories and relationships, plus a conversation state machine that moved interactions through prompting, drafting, refinement, and finalization. At Summer Atlantic Capital I work on the ML core of an anomaly-detection system: temporal sequence modeling over event streams with RNN and Transformer-style approaches, anomaly scoring, a learning-to-rank layer for alert prioritization, and a retrieval-augmented LLM explanation layer served through a versioned FastAPI microservice. In tSearch I built a rubric-driven LLM judging system where individual judges evaluate separate dimensions in parallel and then synthesize an evidence-cited assessment, with "insufficient evidence" as a real output instead of a low score. For agents I use Playwright with TypeScript and Node, calling OpenAI only at narrow call sites so model output never silently drives state. On classical ML I have trained XGBoost models with SHAP interpretation on roughly 10 million survey records, and a PyTorch CNN for facial-landmark prediction at about 95% PCK. I also designed an LLM evaluation framework against a 4,169-case clinical benchmark using stratified sampling.

fields.expected: Notion describes itself as the workspace where teams and agents think together, and that framing is close to the problem I have spent the last year building around: where machine action should stop and human judgment should take over. I built a Playwright-based job-application agent in TypeScript where every application moves through an explicit state machine, mutating capabilities sit behind fail-closed flags like SUBMIT_ENABLED, and free-text and demographic fields are architecturally prevented from being auto-filled. I skipped Workday and iCIMS entirely rather than handling them unreliably. That project taught me that an agent people trust is mostly a design problem about boundaries, not a model problem. Before that, at Intelehealth, I built an evaluation framework comparing LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case standard using stratified sampling, which convinced me that judging whether an output should be trusted is harder than generating it. Agents inside a workspace touch a user's real documents and real work, so those questions are not abstract there. The part I would want to work on is the reliability and evaluation layer around agent behavior in a product people actually use daily.
